source_title: Consumer Financial Protection Bureau Fines Wells Fargo $100 Million for Widespread Illegal Practice of Secretly Opening Unauthorized Accounts
publisher_issuer: U.S. Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB); corroborated by OCC and CNN
company_context: Wells Fargo, one of the largest U.S. banks, built a culture around aggressive cross-selling ('eight is great' product-per-household targets) enforced via sales quotas and compensation incentives. To hit targets, employees secretly opened accounts customers never authorized.
macro_context: Post-crisis banking; intense focus on fee income and cross-sell ratios as a growth metric; heightened regulatory scrutiny of consumer financial practices.
evidence_summary: Spurred by sales targets and incentive compensation, Wells Fargo employees opened more than 2 million unauthorized deposit and credit-card accounts, often funding them by moving customer money without consent and creating fake email enrollments. On September 8, 2016 the CFPB fined the bank $100 million, with $35 million to the OCC and $50 million to the City and County of Los Angeles ($185 million combined), plus customer restitution. The bank had already fired about 5,300 employees. The aggressive cross-sell incentive design was the wrong action that produced widespread fraud and reputational and regulatory damage.

source_backed_metrics.unauthorized_accounts: more than 2 million deposit and credit-card accounts

owner_decision_context: Senior management set and enforced aggressive product-per-customer cross-sell targets tied to incentive compensation, creating pressure that drove employees to fabricate accounts; leadership maintained the incentive structure despite warning signs.
action_taken: Imposed aggressive cross-selling sales quotas and incentive compensation (the wrong action), which drove employees to open millions of unauthorized accounts; the bank then terminated ~5,300 employees and entered consent orders, but the incentive design had already produced systemic fraud.
outcome_evidence: CFPB/OCC/LA consent orders totaling $185 million, ~5,300 firings, mandated restitution and sales-practice overhaul, plus CEO departure and multiyear reputational damage, confirm the incentive action worsened the franchise.
source_limitations: WebFetch of consumerfinance.gov returned HTTP 403; all figures confirmed verbatim across CFPB and OCC .gov press releases and named journalism (CNN, NPR, Congress.gov CRS). Account counts are the bank's own internal-analysis estimates as cited by CFPB; later reviews raised the potential figure to ~3.5 million, not used here.
directly_stated: CFPB fined Wells Fargo $100 million on September 8, 2016; combined penalties $185 million
Employees opened more than 2 million unauthorized deposit and credit-card accounts (~1.5M deposit, 565,443 credit-card applications)
Practices were driven by sales targets and compensation incentives
inferred: The incentive/quota design was the proximate governance failure that produced the fraud
Reputational and leadership consequences extended well beyond the monetary penalties
why_useful_for_opsiq: Outcome-10/15 governance case where a management incentive decision (the action) directly caused systemic fraud and regulatory penalty. Tests whether the engine flags incentive/governance design as the root cause and routes to legal-governance risk re-evaluation rather than treating it as isolated employee misconduct.
